title: Question
text:
You copy-paste an existing chunk to use as a starting point for a new one, but forget to change its label. What happens when you render the document?



Nothing; chunk labels are purely cosmetic and don’t affect rendering.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: chunk labels must be unique, and duplicates cause a rendering error.
Wrong: Quarto does not silently rename duplicate labels.
Correct: chunk labels must be unique within a document; a duplicate causes rendering to fail with an error.
Wrong: this is not how Quarto handles duplicate labels; rendering fails outright.

title: Question
text:
A Quarto document has two R chunks. The first chunk creates an object called x. Can the second chunk use x, without recreating it?



No, each chunk runs in its own isolated environment.
Yes, because all R chunks in a document share a single, continuous session.
Only if both chunks have the same label.
Only if the cache: TRUE option is set on the first chunk.

title: Question
text:

Yes, because all R chunks in a document share a single, continuous session.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: R chunks are not isolated from one another.
Correct: chunks in the same language run in one shared session, so objects persist across chunks in the order they appear.
Wrong: chunk labels identify chunks for referencing and error messages; they don’t control whether objects are shared.
Wrong: caching affects whether a chunk’s computation is rerun on subsequent renders; it isn’t required for objects to be shared within a single render.

You want a chunk’s code to run, but neither the code nor its output should appear anywhere in the rendered document (for example, a setup chunk loading packages). Which option should you use?

eval: FALSEinclude: FALSEecho: FALSEerror: FALSE




Wrong: eval: FALSE prevents the chunk from running at all, so packages would not actually be loaded.
Correct: include: FALSE runs the chunk but hides both the code and any output.
Wrong: echo: FALSE hides only the code; the result would still appear.
Wrong: error: FALSE controls whether rendering stops on an error; it does not hide code or output.





How does Quarto expect chunk options to be written inside an R chunk?

As plain R function calls at the top of the chunk, e.g. set_echo(FALSE).As commented lines starting with #|, placed directly below the chunk header.As arguments inside the curly braces, e.g. {r, echo=FALSE}.As a separate YAML file referenced by the chunk’s label.




Wrong: chunk options are not set through R function calls.
Correct: Quarto chunk options are written as #| commented lines directly below the chunk header.
Wrong: this is the older R Markdown syntax; Quarto uses a different convention.
Wrong: chunk options are written inline in the chunk itself, not in a separate file.

What does wrapping a data frame in knitr::kable() accomplish, compared to letting R print the data frame directly?



It changes the underlying values stored in the data frame.

title: Question

A document has a top-level heading (#), containing a section (##), which itself contains a subsection (###). With number-sections: true set in the YAML header, how would the subsection be numbered?



1
1.1
1.1.1
Subsections are not numbered, only top-level headings are.

text:
1
1.1
1.1.1
Subsections are not numbered, only top-level headings are.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: 1 would be the number given to the top-level heading, not the subsection.
Wrong: 1.1 would be the number given to the section, one level up from the subsection.
Correct: numbering reflects the full heading hierarchy, so the subsection nested two levels deep is numbered 1.1.1.
Wrong: number-sections: true numbers all heading levels, not just the top level.

You reference a figure in your text with @fig-scores, but the figure’s actual chunk label is #| label: fig-score (missing the final “s”). What happens when you render the document?

The figure is renumbered to match the reference automatically.Rendering stops with a fatal error and no document is produced.The reference fails to resolve, and the rendered document shows the broken reference text or a placeholder instead of a number.Quarto automatically matches the closest label and resolves the reference correctly.




Wrong: labels are not automatically adjusted to match an incorrect reference.
Wrong: a mismatched cross-reference does not stop rendering entirely; the rest of the document still renders.
Correct: a cross-reference only resolves if it exactly matches an existing label; otherwise it shows the raw reference text or a placeholder instead of a number.
Wrong: Quarto requires an exact label match; it does not guess or auto-correct mismatched labels.





You embed a regression coefficient directly in your text using the inline expression coef(model)[2], and it renders as “-5.344471517291”. What should you do to make this more suitable for a report?

Wrap the expression in round() or format() before embedding it, e.g. round(coef(model)[2], 2).Move the entire sentence into a separate code chunk instead of using inline code.Nothing; inline results should always show full computational precision.Replace the inline code with a hard-coded number typed directly into the text.




Correct: rounding or formatting the expression keeps the inline result readable, while still updating automatically if the underlying data changes.
Wrong: moving it to a separate chunk doesn’t address the rounding issue, and inline code is specifically meant for embedding results directly in text.
Wrong: unrounded results are usually far more precise than a report needs, and look out of place in a sentence.
Wrong: hard-coding a number defeats the purpose of inline code, since the text would no longer update automatically.

title: Chunks and options
text:
In this tutorial, you will learn the following about code chunks in Quarto:

What code chunks are, and how they share a single execution session.
How to create and label chunks, and why rendering regularly matters.
The most common chunk options, and how they control what appears in your rendered document.




 Back to top

title: Create code chunks
text:
Quarto documents in RStudio can be edited in two modes. In Visual mode, you insert a chunk via Insert → Executable Cell → [language].



Creating chunks through the Visual mode


In Source mode, you create a chunk by typing three backticks followed by the language in curly braces (e.g., ```{r}) and closing it with another three backticks; everything between the fences is executable code.



Creating chunks through the Source mode


Visual mode is a convenient way to build a document with a guided interface, but we recommend working in Source mode as much as possible once you’re comfortable with the syntax.

text:

title: Create code chunks
text:
Rendering Regularly
Because chunks share one session and run top to bottom, it’s good practice to render your document often as you write it, rather than waiting until the end.
Predict: suppose you write five chunks in a row without rendering, and the second chunk has an error. What do you expect to happen when you finally render the whole document?
Explain: rendering stops at the first chunk that fails, and Quarto reports an error pointing to that chunk. This means that you would not learn about the problem until you’d already written three chunks past it, making it harder to pinpoint what went wrong. Rendering after every chunk or two (with the Render button, Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+K, or quarto render yourfile.qmd) catches this immediately instead. You can also run a single chunk on its own with the green play icon (or Ctrl/Cmd+Shift+Enter) to test it before rendering the full document.

title: Create code chunks
text:
Labelling Chunks
Each chunk can be given a label, specified with #| label: <name> immediately inside the chunk. Labels make errors easier to trace back to their source, and are used internally for caching and for naming generated figures and tables. Good labels are unique, short but descriptive, and use only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens or underscores, for example data-load, model-fit, or plot-results.






Common Mistake



Chunk labels must be unique within a document. If two chunks share the same label, Quarto will fail to render and report a duplicate-label error. This is easy to run into if you copy-paste an existing chunk as a starting point for a new one and forget to change its label.








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


Which of the following chunk labels follows good labeling convention: Model Fit!, model_fit_final_version_2, or model-fit?


model-fit. It is short, descriptive, unique, and uses only lowercase letters and a hyphen. Model Fit! uses spaces, capital letters, and a special character, none of which are recommended, and model_fit_final_version_2 is unnecessarily long for a label.

title: Adding structure
text: A well-structured Quarto document helps readers follow your analysis and lets Quarto automatically generate a table of contents, numbered sections, and cross-references. You add structure with headings, numbered elements (figures, tables, equations), and citations.

title: Adding structure
text:
Headings and Section Numbering
Do: Run the following in your own quarto document.
# Main Title

## Section Title

### Subsection Title
See: Quarto interprets these heading levels to build a document hierarchy, reflected in the output and, if enabled, in a table of contents (toc: true in the YAML header).
Predict: if you also add number-sections: true to the YAML header, predict how the three headings above would be numbered.
---
title: "My Analysis Report"
toc: true
number-sections: true
---
Explain: as predicted, headings are numbered according to their hierarchy: 1 for the top-level heading, 1.1 for the section beneath it, and 1.1.1 for the subsection beneath that. This numbering updates automatically as you add, remove, or reorder headings, and each numbered heading can then be cross-referenced elsewhere in the text.

title: Adding structure
text:
Numbering Figures and Equations
Quarto also numbers figures, tables, and equations that have a label. To number a figure, add a label starting with fig- and a caption via fig-cap:
#| label: fig-distribution
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of scores by group."

ggplot(data, aes(x = group, y = score, fill = group)) +
  geom_boxplot()








Figure 1: Distribution of scores by group.





To reference it in text, use the label: See @fig-distribution for an overview. renders as: See Figure 1 for an overview.
Equations are numbered the same way, by adding a label after the closing $$:
$$
E = mc^2
$$ {#eq-myequation}
\[
E = mc^2
\tag{1}\]
Referencing it with @eq-myequation then renders as: Equation 1.






Common Mistake



A cross-reference only works if its target actually has a matching label. If you reference @fig-distribution but the figure’s label is misspelled, missing, or doesn’t start with the required prefix (fig-, tbl-, eq-), Quarto won’t resolve the link. Instead of a number like “Figure 1,” the rendered document will show the broken reference text as-is, or a ?@... placeholder. If a cross-reference isn’t rendering as a number, check the label first.

title: Adding structure
text:
Adding References and Citations
Quarto uses Pandoc’s citation system to cite sources from a bibliography file. In your YAML header, include the path to a .bib file:
---
title: "My Report"
bibliography: references.bib
---
You can then cite works in-text using the @ symbol and the citation key from your .bib file:

@smith2021 → Smith (2021)
[@smith2021; @doe2022] → (Smith 2021; Doe 2022)

To include a bibliography at the end of your document, add a # References heading — Quarto populates it automatically during rendering.








External Resources



For more detail, see Quarto citations








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


You created a figure with #| label: fig-boxplot. What syntax would you use to reference it in your text?


@fig-boxplot. For example: See @fig-boxplot for the distribution of scores.

title: The purpose of Markdown and Quarto
text:
What Is Quarto?
Quarto is an open-source publishing system for creating reproducible documents and websites from plain text files. It combines written content, code, data, and visualizations in a single workflow, supports multiple programming languages (R, Python or Julia), and can render to formats including HTML, PDF, Microsoft Word, and PowerPoint.
Because it integrates writing and computation, Quarto is well-suited for data science reports, research papers, educational materials and presentations, and reproducible analysis pipelines more generally.








Reading



For official documentation, installation instructions, and tutorials, see the Quarto website.
crumbs: The purpose of Markdown and Quarto

title: The purpose of Markdown and Quarto
text:
What is Markdown?
Markdown is a lightweight text formatting language: you write plain text with simple text-based markers (rather than graphical formatting buttons) that get converted into formatted output such as web pages or PDFs. The result is a writing experience that is both human-readable and machine-friendly.
Markdown was created in 2004 to make writing for the web simpler than working directly in HTML, and it has since become a standard tool for technical writing and documentation, forming the foundation of many modern publishing systems — including Quarto.








Reading



Here you find the link to the original Markdown paper.








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


You’re writing a lab report where a table of results needs to update automatically every time you rerun your analysis. Would plain Markdown or Quarto be the right tool for this, and why?


Quarto. Markdown only provides text formatting; it has no way to execute code or generate results. Quarto builds on Markdown by adding a computation layer, so tables and figures can be generated from your analysis and stay in sync with your data.

title: Creating presentations with Quarto
text:
Quarto can also turn a .qmd file into a slide deck. Presentations use the same YAML header and Markdown body as the reports covered in the previous tutorial; they simply render slide-by-slide instead of page-by-page.
Do: Take the Quarto report that you started working on at the documents tutorial. Do you think you could turn it into a slideshow just by changing the format field in the YAML header, or would you need to rewrite the file from scratch?
See: Switching formats is again very simple at the YAML level. In practice you probably want to reorganize the content itself, since a slide holds much less text than a page, and each heading needs to mark where a new slide begins.

title: Creating presentations with Quarto
text:
Example: A Reveal.js Presentation

Example .qmd file
Resulting .html output

Each slide begins with a heading (e.g., ##) or is separated by ---. When rendered, Quarto executes any embedded code chunks and displays their output, such as tables or plots, directly on the slide.
Keep slides concise: aim for clarity, minimal text, and meaningful visuals rather than dense explanations.
Common challenges:

Balancing detail and readability: avoid overloading slides with text or long code blocks.
Consistent design: use concise titles and uniform font sizes.
Cross-platform compatibility: check that revealjs slides display correctly across browsers; pptx output can render differently depending on the software used to open it.

As with reports, revealjs slides are HTML output, so if you’re submitting or sharing slides as a single file, apply the same embed-resources: true setting covered in the previous tutorial.








Reading



Learn more: Quarto Presentations Overview — Reveal.js Presentations — PowerPoint Presentations








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


You have a Quarto HTML report analyzing exam scores and want to present the same analysis as a revealjs slideshow that you can safely email as a single file. What would you change in the YAML header, and what else would you likely still need to adjust in the body of the document?


In the YAML header, change format: html to format: revealjs and keep embed-resources: true so the slideshow stays a single, portable file. In the body, you would still need to reorganize the content into slide-sized chunks, adding headings or --- separators to mark where each new slide begins, and trimming dense text down to the key points.

title: Creating documents with Quarto
text: Quarto lets you create professional reports and papers directly from RStudio, combining code, text, and visualizations in a single reproducible workflow. This tutorial covers the basics of working with Quarto files in RStudio, then walks through creating report-style documents specifically. The next tutorial covers presentations.

title: Creating documents with Quarto
text:
Working with Quarto in RStudio
To start a new Quarto document in RStudio:

Go to File → New File → Quarto Document…
Enter a title, author, and choose a default output format (e.g., HTML, PDF, or Word).
RStudio creates a .qmd file containing a template YAML header and an example code chunk.
Click Render (or use Render on Save) to produce the formatted output.




RStudio Quarto new document dialog (source: https://quarto.org)








Reading



For more information, see the official Quarto documentation: Authoring with RStudio


Every .qmd file has the same basic structure: a YAML header (between --- lines) defining metadata like title and output format, a body written in Markdown, and optional embedded R code chunks.

title: Creating documents with Quarto
text:
YAML: Document Metadata and Configuration
The YAML header is where you tell Quarto how to render your document: what format to produce and which options to apply. It uses a simple key-value structure, enclosed between --- at the start and end of the block.
---
title: "Statistical Analysis of Air Quality Data"
author: "Alex Rivera"
date: "2025-01-01"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    code-fold: true
---
Do: Create a Quarto document on your own computer. In the YAML header of the .qmd file, change format: html to format: pdf in the header. Do you expect this to be a one-line switch, or would you need to change other parts of the document too?
See: For a simple document, changing the target format really can be that simple: the same Markdown body and code chunks are reused. In practice, though, some format-specific options (like code-fold, which is an HTML-only feature) won’t carry over, and PDF output has its own setup requirements, covered below.

title: Creating documents with Quarto
text:
Creating Reports and Papers
Common document output formats include:








Format
Output Type
Typical Use




html
Interactive web report
Exploratory data reports, dashboards


pdf
Print-quality report
Academic papers, formatted submissions


docx
Microsoft Word
Editable reports for collaboration


epub
e-book
Long-form reading materials



Quarto automatically executes embedded code chunks and inserts the resulting tables and plots, so every time you re-render, the analysis and visuals update from your current data.
A few things to keep in mind across formats:

Layout: reports may need page breaks or fixed figure sizing, especially for PDF and Word.
PDF rendering requires a working LaTeX installation (e.g., TinyTeX).
Settings don’t always transfer: an option that works for HTML may not apply to PDF or Word.
Citations are supported via BibTeX, covered later in this module.







Common Mistake



By default, a rendered HTML report can reference supporting files, such as separately saved images, rather than embedding everything into the single .html file. If you then hand in or share only that .html file, without its supporting files, it can open broken or missing content for whoever receives it. To avoid this, set your document to be self-contained by adding embed-resources: true under your HTML format options:
format:
  html:
    embed-resources: true
This produces a single, fully portable .html file with everything, including plots and images, embedded inside it. This is important whenever you’re submitting a report as one file, for example for a homework assignment.










Reading



Learn more: Quarto Document Formats








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


Write a YAML header for an HTML report titled “Analysis Report,” with a table of contents, that is safe to hand in as a single file.


---
title: "Analysis Report"
format:
  html:
    toc: true
    embed-resources: true
---
The toc: true option adds a table of contents, and embed-resources: true ensures the rendered .html file is self-contained, so it can be shared or submitted on its own.

title: Differences between Quarto and Markdown
text:
Markdown and Quarto operate at different levels. Markdown is a markup language: plain text with lightweight formatting instructions for elements like headings, lists, and emphasis. It has no support for code execution, metadata, or dynamic output, which makes it ideal for static content like documentation or notes, but not for combining text with live results.
Quarto builds on Markdown to add a document generation and publishing workflow. It extends Markdown’s syntax with tools for executing embedded code, managing metadata, and rendering to multiple output formats such as HTML, PDF, and slides.
In short, Markdown provides the structure, while Quarto provides the workflow that ties narrative, computation, and presentation together.








Layer
Example
Purpose




Language layer
Markdown
Provide the text structure, document content, and basic formatting syntax.


Processing layer
Quarto
Interpret Markdown, integrate executable code, and render everything into polished output formats such as HTML or PDF.


Computation layer
R (and optionally Python, Julia)
Perform analysis, generate tables and plots, and supply dynamic results embedded into the rendered document.



RStudio ties these three layers together in one environment: Markdown structures the text, Quarto renders it and executes the embedded code, and R supplies the actual computation. This lets you write, analyze, and present your work within a single, seamless workflow.






Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


A colleague asks you to convert your Quarto report into a plain Markdown file, so they can drop it into a different publishing system. Would you lose anything in the process, and if so, what?


Yes. You would lose the computation layer: any embedded code chunks, and the tables, figures, or inline results they generate, since Markdown alone cannot execute code. Only the plain narrative text and static formatting would survive the conversion.








 Back to top

title: Inline code and results
text: Inline code lets you execute an R expression directly within your narrative text, so a report always reflects the current data or computation, without manually copying results in.

title: Inline code and results
text:
Syntax for Inline Code
Inline code is written with a single pair of backticks, starting with the language identifier:
Do: Run this code inline where you are writing text in your own Quarto document.

`r 2 + 2`

See: including this in a sentence runs the code and prints only the result: 4.
Predict: now suppose a previous chunk already created an object, mean_score <- mean(c(5, 10, 15)). Before looking below, predict what the following inline code will show once rendered: the code itself, or the number it evaluates to?

`r mean_score`

Explain: as predicted, only the result appears: “The average score is 10.” The expression is evaluated at render time, and only its result is shown; you can use any valid R expression, including objects created in earlier chunks.

title: Inline code and results
text:
Using Inline Code in Text
Inline code works well for numbers that should always match the current analysis. For example, the syntax

The mean mpg is `r round(mean(mtcars$mpg), 1)`.

renders as: The mean mpg is 20.1. The same approach works for model results:

The regression slope is `r round(coef(lm(mpg ~ wt, data = mtcars))[2], 2)`.

renders as: The regression slope is -5.34.






Common Mistake



Raw inline results are often much longer or messier than you’d want in a sentence: an unrounded slope like -5.344471517... looks out of place in a report. Always round (round()) or format (format()) numeric results before embedding them, rather than leaving the raw computed value to print as-is.








Practice Exercise



Create a numeric vector called scores with a few values of your choice, then compute its mean rounded to 1 decimal place, the way you would for an inline result.

 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



scores <- c(72.456, 88.219, 91.038, 65.774)
round(mean(scores), 1)

[1] 79.4


If this were an inline expression in a report, e.g.

The average score is `r round(mean(scores), 1)`.

it would render as: “The average score is 79.4.” Rounding keeps the embedded result readable in a sentence, rather than printing several unnecessary decimal places.

title: Writing text
text:
Quarto builds on Pandoc Markdown, which supports inline formatting for emphasis, code, strikethrough, and superscript/subscript.
Do: Run this in your own Quarto document and see how it looks.
*italics*
**bold**
See: In visual mode, or when rendering the document, you should see this:
italics bold
Predict: now suppose you wrap a word in three asterisks instead of one or two, like ***word***. Do you expect this to render as italics, bold, or both combined?
Explain:
***bold italics***
bold italics
As predicted, combining the two markers combines both effects.
A few other inline formatting options are useful to know:

Strikethrough: ~~text~~ → text.
Inline (verbatim) code: enclose text in backticks, e.g. `my_var <- 10` → my_var <- 10.
Superscript / subscript: superscript^2^ → superscript², subscript~2~ → subscript₂.

title: Writing text
text:
Lists
Quarto supports unordered and ordered lists, including nested lists.

Unordered lists start lines with *, +, or -:
* Item A
* Item B
  + Sub-item B1
* Item C

Item A
Item B

Sub-item B1

Item C

Ordered lists use numbers followed by a dot:
1. First step
2. Second step
3. Third step

First step
Second step
Third step

Task lists use [ ] or [x]:
- [ ] Task 1
- [x] Task 2 (done)

Task 1
Task 2 (done)








Common Mistake



Quarto requires a blank line before a list for it to render correctly. Without it, the list items may appear as ordinary text rather than a formatted list. If a list isn’t rendering the way you expect, check for a missing blank line above it first.

title: Writing text
text:
Links and Equations

Inline link: [Quarto](https://quarto.org) → Quarto
Autolink URL: <https://quarto.org> → https://quarto.org

Quarto supports LaTeX-style math using $ and $$ delimiters:

Inline math: This is inline: $E = mc^2$. → This is inline: \(E = mc^2\).
Display math, on its own centered line:
$$
E = mc^2
$$
\[
E = mc^2
\]









External Resources



Markdown basics








Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


Write the Markdown syntax for a sentence that is both bold and italicized, ending with a variable name written as verbatim code, x, followed by a superscript 2.


***This sentence is bold and italicized***, using `x`^2^.
This sentence is bold and italicized, using x2.

title: Figures
text: Figures are essential for visualizing data. Quarto supports figures generated from R code as well as external images, with chunk options and Markdown attributes controlling captions, size, and placement.

title: Figures
text:
Figures Generated from R
Do: Run the code below in your own Quarto document. It sets four chunk options:

label: fig-scores — a label enabling this figure to be cross-referenced elsewhere as @fig-scores
fig-cap — the figure’s caption
fig-width / fig-height — the figure’s dimensions, in inches


library(ggplot2)

data <- data.frame(
  Group = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Score = c(5.2, 6.8, 4.9)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = Group, y = Score, fill = Group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Boxplot of scores by group





See: the resulting figure, with the caption and dimensions from the chunk options applied.
Predict: if you add fig-align: "center" to this same chunk, what do you expect to change: the figure’s content and size, or something else?
Explain: fig-align only changes the figure’s horizontal placement on the page (left/center/right); the plot itself, its caption, and its dimensions stay exactly the same. Chunk options that control appearance are independent of one another, much like the hist()/plot() styling options covered in the visualization module.
When possible, export figures as vector graphics (PDF or SVG) rather than raster formats (PNG, JPEG): vector graphics stay crisp at any zoom level or print size, while raster images can look blurry or pixelated when scaled up.

title: Figures
text:
External Images
Local and web images can also be included, using Markdown’s image syntax.
Local images, referenced with a project-relative path (leading /):
![Caption text](/assets/images/ecrins_pano.jpg){#fig-local width=50%}






Figure 2: Caption text



Web images, linked directly by URL:
![Quarto logo](https://quarto.org/quarto.png){width=200px}



Quarto logo


Both accept the same {#fig-label width=...} attributes as R-generated figures, so they can be sized and cross-referenced the same way.






Common Mistake



A local image path that works on one page can break on another if it’s a plain relative path (e.g., images/photo.jpg), since Quarto resolves it relative to that page’s own folder — the same class of path problem covered for bibliography files earlier in this module. For images, a leading / reliably resolves the path from the project root regardless of which page includes it, so prefer /assets/images/photo.jpg over a bare relative path.

title: Figures
text:
Referencing Figures in Text
Once a figure has a label, reference it anywhere in the text with @:
As shown in @fig-scores, group B has the highest score.
As shown in Figure 1, group B has the highest score.








External Resources



Quarto documentation on figures








Practice Exercise



Create a labeled, captioned bar plot with ggplot2 showing the Score for each Group in the data frame from the example above, sized 5 by 3 inches.

 Interactive Editor Hint Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.


The plot itself can be built and tested here with ggplot2. In an actual .qmd file, you would also add these chunk options above the code to control the label, caption, and size:
#| label: fig-mine
#| fig-cap: "Your caption here"
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3



library(ggplot2)

data <- data.frame(
  Group = c("A", "B", "C"),
  Score = c(5.2, 6.8, 4.9)
)

ggplot(data, aes(x = Group, y = Score, fill = Group)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_minimal()








In a real .qmd file, this chunk would also carry #| label: fig-mine, #| fig-cap: "Your caption here", #| fig-width: 5, and #| fig-height: 3 as chunk options above the code.

title: Tables
text: Tables are a common way to summarize data in reports. Quarto can produce tables directly in Markdown or dynamically from R. Clear, readable tables make your documents more professional and easier to follow.

title: Introduction to code chunks
text:
In a Quarto document, code chunks are self-contained blocks of executable code embedded within the text. Each chunk is delimited by a fenced syntax (triple backticks followed by a language label, such as {r}) telling Quarto which language engine to use. When you render the document, Quarto runs each chunk, captures its output, such as console text, tables and plots, and inserts that output directly into the document at the chunk’s position.
Chunks aren’t limited to R: a single document can mix chunks written in R, Python, Julia, or other supported languages.

title: Introduction to code chunks
text:
In a Quarto document, code chunks are self-contained blocks of executable code embedded within the text. Each chunk is delimited by a fenced syntax (triple backticks followed by a language label, such as {r}) telling Quarto which language engine to use. When you render the document, Quarto runs each chunk, captures its output, such as console text, tables and plots, and inserts that output directly into the document at the chunk’s position.
Chunks aren’t limited to R: a single document can mix chunks written in R, Python, Julia, or other supported languages.

title: Introduction to code chunks
text:
Chunks Share One Session
Do: Carefully look at the three chunks below that all use R in a different way.
First chunk:

# Create a small dataset
set.seed(123)
data <- data.frame(
  group = rep(c("A", "B"), each = 10),
  score = c(rnorm(10, mean = 75, sd = 5),
            rnorm(10, mean = 82, sd = 6))
)

# Display a quick summary of the data
summary(data$score)

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  68.67   73.58   78.91   79.31   84.22   92.72 


Second chunk:

# Use the dataset created in the previous chunk
model <- lm(score ~ group, data = data)

# Display regression results
summary(model)


Call:
lm(formula = score ~ group, data = data)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-13.0514  -3.3335   0.1264   2.1877   9.4697 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   75.373      1.754  42.970  < 2e-16 ***
groupB         7.879      2.481   3.176  0.00523 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 5.547 on 18 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.3591,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3235 
F-statistic: 10.09 on 1 and 18 DF,  p-value: 0.005231


Third chunk:





Distribution of scores by group.




See: As you can see, an object created in the first chunk is still available by the time the second or third chunk runs. For example, data and model are both still available in the third chunk, even though neither was created here. All R chunks in a document run in the same, shared session, so objects created in one chunk persist and can be reused in any chunk that comes after it, much like running code line by line in a single R script.
This has a practical consequence: chunks are not independent snippets to be formatted individually. They are steps in one continuous computation, executed top to bottom.






Common Mistake



Because chunks share a session, code that runs fine when you execute chunks one at a time in RStudio can still fail on a full render if an earlier chunk was skipped, reordered, or edited since you last ran it. Rendering the whole document from a clean session, covered next, is the only way to be sure every chunk still works in the order it actually appears.








Practice Exercise



In the editor below, write two short pieces of code to mimic how two chunks in the same document would behave.

First, create a numeric vector called temperatures containing a few values of your choice.
Then, on a new line, compute the mean of temperatures.

Run both lines together and confirm that the second line can access the object created by the first.

 Interactive Editor Solution



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.



# "Chunk" 1: create an object
temperatures <- c(18, 21, 19, 23, 17)

# "Chunk" 2: reuse the object created above
mean(temperatures)

[1] 19.6


Running these two steps in sequence in the same session mirrors what happens across two chunks in a real Quarto document: temperatures is created in the first step and is still available in the second, without being redefined.

title: Chunk options
text:
Chunk options control how a chunk’s code is executed and how its results appear in the rendered document — whether the code is shown, whether messages are printed, how figures are sized, and more.








External Resources



Quarto documentation on chunk options


Quarto specifies chunk options as commented lines beginning with #|, directly below the chunk header, rather than inline in the curly braces:
#| label: data-summary
#| echo: TRUE
#| message: FALSE

title: Chunk options
text:
Chunk options control how a chunk’s code is executed and how its results appear in the rendered document — whether the code is shown, whether messages are printed, how figures are sized, and more.








External Resources



Quarto documentation on chunk options


Quarto specifies chunk options as commented lines beginning with #|, directly below the chunk header, rather than inline in the curly braces:
#| label: data-summary
#| echo: TRUE
#| message: FALSE

title: Chunk options
text:
Display Control: echo
The echo option controls whether the chunk’s source code itself appears in the rendered document; the result is always shown regardless.
Predict: given the chunk below sets echo: FALSE, will the rendered document show the code, the result, both, or neither?
#| echo: FALSE
mean(c(5, 10, 15))


[1] 10


Explain: as shown above, only the result (10) appears; the mean(c(5, 10, 15)) code itself is hidden. results, warning, and message work the same way for their respective content: each independently controls whether that one type of output is shown, without affecting whether the code or other outputs appear.






Common Mistake



echo: FALSE and include: FALSE are easy to confuse. echo: FALSE hides only the code, while the result (text, table, or plot) still appears. include: FALSE hides both code and result while still running the chunk. Use include: FALSE for setup chunks (like loading packages) that should run silently, and echo: FALSE when you want the reader to see a result without the code that produced it.

title: Chunk options
text:
Execution Options

eval determines whether the chunk is executed at all (TRUE/FALSE).
error determines whether rendering continues if the chunk throws an error (TRUE) or stops (FALSE).

A setup chunk that loads packages but shouldn’t appear in the final report combines these ideas:
#| label: setup
#| include: FALSE

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

title: Chunk options
text:
Figure and Table Options
When a chunk produces a plot or table, these options control its appearance:

fig-cap adds a caption.
fig-width / fig-height set the dimensions, in inches.
fig-align sets the alignment ("left", "center", "right").

#| label: visualization
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig-cap: "Distribution of scores by group."

title: Chunk options
text:
Caching
Setting cache: TRUE saves a chunk’s results so they don’t need to be recomputed on every render, unless the code itself changes. This is useful for slow computations in large documents, but remember to clear the cache if the underlying data changes without the code changing.






Practice Exercise




 Question Solution


You want a chunk’s plot to appear in the rendered report, captioned “Figure 1: Distribution of scores,” but without showing the ggplot code that created it. Which two chunk options do you need, and what would you set them to?


echo: FALSE to hide the code while keeping the plot, and fig-cap: "Figure 1: Distribution of scores" to add the caption.

title: Knowledge Quiz: Quarto and Markdown
text:
Note




Click the check-mark button to check your answer.
Click the question-mark button to see an explanation of the solution.






Which capability does Quarto have that plain Markdown lacks?

Adding hyperlinks to a document.Applying bold or italic emphasis to text.Executing code and embedding the resulting output in a document.Formatting text with headings and lists.




Wrong: hyperlinks are supported by Markdown alone.
Wrong: emphasis (bold/italic) is a core Markdown feature.
Correct: Markdown has no computation layer; Quarto adds the ability to execute code and embed dynamic results.
Wrong: heading and list formatting is a core Markdown feature, available without Quarto.





What is the primary purpose of the YAML header at the top of a Quarto document?

To execute the document’s R code.To write the narrative text that appears in the rendered document.To list the keyboard shortcuts available in RStudio.To define metadata and rendering options, such as the title and output format.




Wrong: R code is executed in code chunks in the document body, not in the YAML header.
Wrong: narrative text belongs in the Markdown body, not the YAML header.
Wrong: the YAML header has nothing to do with RStudio keyboard shortcuts.
Correct: the YAML header configures metadata (title, author) and rendering options (output format, table of contents, etc.).





You render an HTML report and want to email just the single .html file to your instructor as a homework submission. Which YAML option should you add to make sure all images and plots are embedded directly in that file, rather than referenced externally?

number-sections: truetoc: truecode-fold: trueembed-resources: true




Wrong: number-sections adds section numbering; it has no effect on whether resources are embedded.
Wrong: toc adds a table of contents; it has no effect on whether resources are embedded.
Wrong: code-fold controls whether code is collapsible; it has no effect on whether resources are embedded.
Correct: embed-resources: true embeds all supporting files, such as images and plots, directly into a single, portable .html file.





You already have a Quarto report rendered as HTML and want to turn the same analysis into a revealjs slideshow. What is the most direct way to do this?

Change the format field in the YAML header from html to revealjs.Rewrite the entire file from scratch using slide-specific syntax.Convert the file to PDF first, then to slides.Manually copy each paragraph into a separate PowerPoint file.




Correct: changing format to revealjs is the key step, though the content typically still needs to be reorganized into slide-sized chunks.
Wrong: presentations reuse the same YAML and Markdown structure as documents; a full rewrite isn’t necessary.
Wrong: there is no need to convert to PDF as an intermediate step.
Wrong: this bypasses Quarto entirely and isn’t how Quarto presentations are created.







 Back to top

title: Question
text:
You embed a regression coefficient directly in your text using the inline expression coef(model)[2], and it renders as “-5.344471517291”. What should you do to make this more suitable for a report?



Nothing; inline results should always show full computational precision.
Wrap the expression in round() or format() before embedding it, e.g. round(coef(model)[2], 2).
Replace the inline code with a hard-coded number typed directly into the text.
Move the entire sentence into a separate code chunk instead of using inline code.

title: Question
text:
Nothing; inline results should always show full computational precision.
Wrap the expression in round() or format() before embedding it, e.g. round(coef(model)[2], 2).
Replace the inline code with a hard-coded number typed directly into the text.
Move the entire sentence into a separate code chunk instead of using inline code.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: unrounded results are usually far more precise than a report needs, and look out of place in a sentence.
Correct: rounding or formatting the expression keeps the inline result readable, while still updating automatically if the underlying data changes.
Wrong: hard-coding a number defeats the purpose of inline code, since the text would no longer update automatically.
Wrong: moving it to a separate chunk doesn’t address the rounding issue, and inline code is specifically meant for embedding results directly in text.

title: Question
text:
You reference a figure in your text with @fig-scores, but the figure’s actual chunk label is #| label: fig-score (missing the final “s”). What happens when you render the document?



Quarto automatically matches the closest label and resolves the reference correctly.
The reference fails to resolve, and the rendered document shows the broken reference text or a placeholder instead of a number.
Rendering stops with a fatal error and no document is produced.
The figure is renumbered to match the reference automatically.

title: Question
text:
Quarto automatically matches the closest label and resolves the reference correctly.
The reference fails to resolve, and the rendered document shows the broken reference text or a placeholder instead of a number.
Rendering stops with a fatal error and no document is produced.
The figure is renumbered to match the reference automatically.

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: Quarto requires an exact label match; it does not guess or auto-correct mismatched labels.
Correct: a cross-reference only resolves if it exactly matches an existing label; otherwise it shows the raw reference text or a placeholder instead of a number.
Wrong: a mismatched cross-reference does not stop rendering entirely; the rest of the document still renders.
Wrong: labels are not automatically adjusted to match an incorrect reference.

title: Knowledge Quiz: Presenting Output
text:
Note




Click the check-mark button to check your answer.
Click the question-mark button to see an explanation of the solution.






What does wrapping a data frame in knitr::kable() accomplish, compared to letting R print the data frame directly?

It renders the data as a properly formatted table matching the document’s style, rather than R’s plain console-style printout.It converts the data frame into a figure.It changes the underlying values stored in the data frame.It automatically rounds every numeric column to two decimal places.




Correct: kable() produces a clean, document-formatted table instead of R’s raw console output.
Wrong: kable() produces a table, not a figure.
Wrong: kable() only changes how the data is displayed, not the underlying values.
Wrong: kable() does not automatically round values; rounding must be done separately if desired.





What do the fig-width and fig-height chunk options control?

The color palette used in the plot.The dimensions of the rendered figure, in inches.Whether the figure’s code is shown alongside the plot.The caption text shown below the figure.




Wrong: the color palette is determined by the plotting code itself, not by these chunk options.
Correct: fig-width and fig-height set the rendered figure’s dimensions, in inches.
Wrong: showing or hiding code is controlled by echo, not the figure sizing options.
Wrong: the caption is set with fig-cap, not fig-width/fig-height.





You include a local image in a page using a plain relative path, images/photo.jpg. The image displays correctly on that page, but breaks when the same image is included from a page in a different folder. What is the most reliable fix?

Move the image next to every page that uses it.Rename the image file.Convert the image to a different file format.Use a project-relative path with a leading slash, e.g. /assets/images/photo.jpg.




Wrong: duplicating the image across folders works but isn’t a reliable or maintainable fix.
Wrong: renaming the file doesn’t address how the path is resolved.
Wrong: the file format has no bearing on how the path is resolved.
Correct: a leading / makes the path resolve from the project root regardless of which page includes it.





Why is it generally recommended to export figures as vector graphics (e.g., PDF or SVG) rather than a raster format (e.g., PNG or JPEG) for a report?

Vector graphics load faster in a web browser than raster images.Vector formats are the only ones supported by Quarto.Vector graphics render crisply at any zoom level or print size, while raster images can look blurry or pixelated when scaled up.Vector formats always produce smaller file sizes than raster formats.




Wrong: load time depends on file size and complexity, not simply on vector versus raster format.
Wrong: Quarto supports both vector and raster image formats.
Correct: vector graphics scale without loss of quality, so they stay sharp when zoomed in or printed at a larger size, unlike raster images.
Wrong: file size depends on the image’s complexity, not simply on whether it’s vector or raster.

title: Question
text:
How does Quarto expect chunk options to be written inside an R chunk?



As arguments inside the curly braces, e.g. {r, echo=FALSE}.
As commented lines starting with #|, placed directly below the chunk header.
As a separate YAML file referenced by the chunk’s label.
As plain R function calls at the top of the chunk, e.g. set_echo(FALSE).

title: Question
text:
As arguments inside the curly braces, e.g. {r, echo=FALSE}.
As commented lines starting with #|, placed directly below the chunk header.
As a separate YAML file referenced by the chunk’s label.
As plain R function calls at the top of the chunk, e.g. set_echo(FALSE).

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: this is the older R Markdown syntax; Quarto uses a different convention.
Correct: Quarto chunk options are written as #| commented lines directly below the chunk header.
Wrong: chunk options are written inline in the chunk itself, not in a separate file.
Wrong: chunk options are not set through R function calls.

title: Question
text:
You want a chunk’s code to run, but neither the code nor its output should appear anywhere in the rendered document (for example, a setup chunk loading packages). Which option should you use?



echo: FALSE
eval: FALSE
include: FALSE
error: FALSE

title: Question
text:
echo: FALSE
eval: FALSE
include: FALSE
error: FALSE

title: Question
text:
Answerlist

Wrong: echo: FALSE hides only the code; the result would still appear.
Wrong: eval: FALSE prevents the chunk from running at all, so packages would not actually be loaded.
Correct: include: FALSE runs the chunk but hides both the code and any output.
Wrong: error: FALSE controls whether rendering stops on an error; it does not hide code or output.
